one_liner: Zero-dependency Rust derive serializer whose schemaless binary format encodes ~3.8x and decodes ~1.6x faster than prost on logs.
what_it_does: nanoserde is a fork of makepad-tinyserde. It adds #[derive(SerBin, DeBin)] to Rust structs and enums, plus JSON and RON derives (TOML support has no derive), and keeps syn, quote and proc_macro2 out of the build tree. The binary API is two traits: ser_bin(&self, &mut Vec<u8>) or serialize_bin() -> Vec<u8> for encoding, and de_bin(&mut offset, &[u8]) or deserialize_bin(&[u8]) -> Result<T, DeBinErr> for decoding. It cannot stand in for protobuf where interop matters, because there is no .proto schema, no field tags and no implementation in any other language: the Rust type definition is the format.
how_it_is_fast: There is no intermediate data model like serde's Serializer/Visitor layer. Each derive is a hand-written token parser that emits straight-line code calling ser_bin/de_bin on every field in declaration order. The wire format is the plain struct layout: integers and floats are fixed-width little-endian bytes appended with extend_from_slice, strings and collections get a u64 length prefix, Option is a 1-byte tag, and enum variants are a u16 index. There are no field tags, no varints and no pass to compute the size first. Decoding is a bounds-checked cursor (offset: &mut usize) over the input slice. That removes protobuf's per-field tag and varint work, at the cost of larger output than varint formats and no schema evolution.
when_to_use: Rust-to-Rust messages or save files where both sides build from the same struct definitions and you want 3.8-6.5x faster encoding than prost without a .proto step (log 190.59 us vs 731.23 us; minecraft_savedata 165.05 us vs 1.0006 ms; mk48 701.90 us vs 4.5619 ms).

Game, wasm32 or small-binary projects where compile time and dependency count matter. The only dependency is nanoserde's own proc-macro crate, and CI builds wasm32-unknown-unknown, Windows (MSVC and GNU), macOS x86_64 and Linux.
no_std + alloc targets: turning off the default std feature builds the crate as no_std, without the HashMap/HashSet/SystemTime impls.
Records full of strings and structs (logs, player saves) where you also want JSON or RON from the same small dependency, and decode times around 1.5-1.7 ms on these datasets are acceptable.
when_not_to_use: Cross-language or long-lived data. Fields are positional with no tags, enum variants are u16 indices in declaration order, and the binary format does not support #[nserde(default)]. Adding, removing or reordering a field or variant makes previously written bytes unreadable.

Bulk numeric arrays or byte blobs. Vec<T> is encoded element by element, with no memcpy path for Vec<u8> or Vec<f32>. On the mesh dataset it serializes in 1.3246 ms, against 147.88 us for wincode and 142.33 us for savefile, and deserializes in 824.47 us against about 144 us.

Size-sensitive links. Fixed-width integers and 8-byte length prefixes make its log output 18% larger than prost's (1,045,784 vs 884,628 B) and about 1.5-1.9x larger than bitcode's on log and mk48 (703,710 B; 1,812,404 vs 971,318 B). Varint lengths (issue #97) would need a breaking major release.

Untrusted input. Vec, HashSet and HashMap decoding call with_capacity(len) with a length read from the input before checking that enough bytes remain. A crafted length prefix can therefore force a huge allocation (abort) or a capacity-overflow panic. This comes from reading the source; no fuzzing or advisory was found.

Zero-copy or streaming I/O. There is no borrowed (&str/&[u8]) decoding (the shootout marks Borrow as unsupported), and there is no io::Read/io::Write API: issue #23 is open, and the maintainers declined the change in #103.

integration.dependencies: none beyond its own nanoserde-derive proc-macro crate (no syn/quote/proc_macro2)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.81 (rust-version in Cargo.toml), edition 2021; CI tests the no_std configuration on nightly only
integration.platforms: any; the format is explicitly little-endian. CI builds x86_64 Linux, x86_64 Windows (MSVC and GNU), x86_64 macOS and wasm32-unknown-unknown, but runs tests only on x86_64 Linux
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the binary API is stateless functions over &self and &[u8] with no global state (from source)

gotchas: Decoding is lenient: any non-zero byte decodes as bool true, and any Option tag other than 1 decodes as None, so corrupted input can be accepted instead of rejected.
usize and all lengths are written as u64. On 32-bit targets such as wasm32 the decoded value is cast with 'as usize', which silently truncates anything above u32::MAX.
An unknown enum discriminant is reported at offset 0 rather than its real position. Derive parse failures show up as proc-macro panics (unimplemented!) instead of errors pointing at the source.

crates.io is still at 0.2.1 (2025-03-22), the benchmarked version; master is at 0.2.2 and holds later fixes, such as the UnknownDiscriminant error and compile errors on unknown #[nserde] attributes, that are not published. nanoserde-derive is MIT-only while nanoserde is MIT OR Apache-2.0, and the published derive crate ships without a license file (issue #156).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick nanoserde over wincode, savefile or bitcode when a dependency-free build tree and binary+JSON+RON in one crate matter more than the last 30-40% of speed. On log, wincode serializes in 137.05 us and deserializes in 1.4166 ms at the same output size (1,045,784 B), savefile serializes in 154.62 us, and bitcode is both faster (96.821 us / 1.1452 ms) and 33% smaller. For numeric arrays pick wincode or savefile; if you need schema evolution, stay on a tagged format.
verified_claims_summary: The numbers come from djkoloski's rust_serialization_benchmark: Criterion, run 2026-09-10, rustc 1.100.0-nightly with LLVM 23.1.1, lto = true, on a 4-vCPU AMD EPYC 9V74 VM. On the log set nanoserde 0.2.1 serialized in 190.59 us against prost 0.14.4's 731.23 us encode-only (~3.8x; ~9.9x against populate+encode) and deserialized in 1.6898 ms against 2.6802 ms (~1.6x). It also beat prost on mesh (1.3246 ms vs 5.8939 ms serialize, 824.47 us vs 10.253 ms deserialize), minecraft_savedata and mk48; all of these compare Rust crates, not C++ libprotobuf.
status_note: Actively maintained (commits through September 2026, 911 stars, ~1.7M crates.io downloads), dual MIT/Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor. However, the last crates.io release is 0.2.1 from March 2025, and the maintainer says they prioritize 'simple + no dependency + safe over as fast as possible'.
